blocks.text: Arrays and linked lists put things in a **line**. A lot of the world isn't a line — it **branches**. And branching turns out to be the key to searching huge amounts of data in a handful of steps. Those are the two big reasons trees exist.
1. The world is full of hierarchies
Whenever things contain other things, you have a tree:

blocks.alt: Three everyday trees. A file system: the folder Home contains Documents and Photos, and Documents contains cv.pdf and notes.txt. A web page: html contains head and body, and body contains h1 and p. An arithmetic expression: (2 + 3) times 4 is a tree with times at the root, plus on the left over 2 and 3, and 4 on the right.

items: **The page you're reading** — every web page is a tree of HTML elements (the DOM).
**Compilers** — your code is parsed into a *syntax tree*; `(2 + 3) × 4` becomes the tree on the right, and evaluating it is a tree walk.
**Decisions** — a decision tree asks one yes/no question per node; a game AI explores a tree of possible moves.
**Organisation charts, family trees, menus, comment threads…**

blocks.text: Only trees with **at most two** children per node are *binary* trees, and many of these hierarchies have more. But binary trees are the ones interviews and data structure libraries are built on, and everything you learn here carries over.
2. Fast search: throw away half at every step

Suppose a tree keeps one simple rule at every node: **everything in the left subtree is smaller, everything in the right subtree is bigger**. That's a **binary search tree** (BST). To find a value, compare it with the root — and you know which side it must be on. The other side, with possibly half the data, is never looked at.

blocks.alt: Searching for 7 in a binary search tree with root 8. 7 is less than 8, so go left to 3; 7 is greater than 3, so go right to 6; 7 is greater than 6, so go right and find 7. The subtrees not taken are greyed out. Only 4 of 9 nodes are checked.

blocks.caption: Search for a value that isn't there: you still only walk one path.

blocks.text: The cost is the number of levels walked: the tree's **height**. A balanced tree doubles its capacity with every level, so its height is about **log₂ n**: 20 levels hold a million values, 30 hold a billion.

blocks.alt: The same seven values in two shapes. Balanced, the tree has height 2 and any value is at most 3 checks away. Inserted in sorted order, the tree degenerates into a chain of height 6 — no better than a linked list.

blocks.text: A tree's speed depends entirely on its **shape**. That's why real libraries use **self-balancing** trees (red-black trees in Java's `TreeMap` and C++'s `std::map`, B-trees in databases) that rotate nodes to keep the height near log n after every insert and delete.
Why not a sorted array, or a hash table?

blocks.alt: A comparison of costs. Sorted array: search O(log n) with binary search, but insert or delete O(n) because elements shift. Linked list: search O(n), insert O(1) once you are at the spot. Hash table: search, insert, delete O(1) on average, but no order: no smallest, no range queries. Balanced binary search tree: search, insert and delete all O(log n), and the values stay in sorted order.

blocks.text: A balanced BST is the all-rounder: nearly as fast as a hash table, and it also answers **ordered** questions — the smallest value, the next bigger key, every value between 10 and 20 — which hashing can't. Trees also power **heaps** (priority queues), **tries** (autocomplete) and **segment trees** (range queries), all of which you'll meet later.

items: Trees model **hierarchies**: folders, web pages, syntax trees, decisions.
A **binary search tree** discards a whole subtree with every comparison, so search costs O(height).
Balanced trees have height **≈ log₂ n** (20 levels for a million items); skewed trees degrade to a linked list.
Balanced BSTs give O(log n) search, insert and delete **and** keep the data in order.
